title: Word on the Day of the Dormition
attribution_note: Translated for this edition from the Russian of St Tikhon of Zadonsk (public domain), from the Words Spoken to the Voronezh Flock — the twelve long sermons he preached as bishop of Voronezh, 1763–1767. The Russian text the translation was made from is kept in the repository. Preached 1765; the manuscript, corrected in the saint's own hand, was kept at the Sophia Usman monastery.

pairs.en: A bright and altogether welcome spectacle I see before me today, my hearers. I see, gathered in this splendid temple, a great multitude of people of every rank and both sexes come together. I see the sacred order of the ministers of God Most High; I see the governors of the city and the commanders of its armies; I see the soldiers, defenders of the holy Church and of the Fatherland. I see those who sit in the courts of judgment, rendering the judgment of God, and their fellow-workers who labour day and night, unsleeping, for the good of the Fatherland and the common welfare. I see the worthy merchants, so useful to the Fatherland. I see, in short, a multitude of people of every calling and rank; I see the old and the young. All of you, I trust, have been gathered to this holy place by the sacred and glorious memory of the Mother of God. And for you all the holy Church now begins to sing — like a second Miriam, with choirs and spiritual songs.

On this day the living temple of the Godhead, the Mother of life that never grows old, passed from the things of earth to the things of heaven. On this day *“the Queen stood at the right hand of the King, arrayed in a vesture wrought with gold”* [Psalm 44:10]. To this spiritual feast you have come in great numbers. Good and praiseworthy is your intention; your labour is not in vain. By this — by the honour you show her holy memory — your love and zeal for the Mother of God are known. And by this your faith is known too: that though she has passed from earth to the things of heaven, she *“did not forsake the world in her falling asleep,”* but unceasingly intercedes for all with her Son and God. Stand firm, then, in your faith.

Wishing to add still more joy to this spiritual festival, I will speak with you about the power and working of faith, so that, once you understand what faith is, you may the more readily bring forth its fruits. My discourse falls into two parts. First: what faith is, and what its fruits are. Second: from what source faith is acquired and increased.

sections.heading: Faith is the root, life the tree

pairs.en: A person who thinks in a spiritual way is like a tree, my hearers. A tree depends entirely on its root: as the root is, so is the tree. And what the root is to the tree, faith is to the spiritually-minded person: as faith is within, so is the person. The more a tree's root spreads and goes deep, the more the tree grows and rises, the more its branches spread and its fruit multiplies. So too, the more faith deepens and increases in a person, the more that person grows spiritually, rises up, and brings forth ever more numerous spiritual fruits. Such a spiritual person we all call a great person — even if by natural age he is still small, even if he holds the very lowest rank, even if the whole world despises and spits upon him.

It is such a person the God-inspired psalmist describes: *“He shall be like a tree planted by the streams of water, which yields its fruit in its season, and whose leaf does not wither; and whatever he does shall prosper”* [Psalm 1:3]. And again: *“The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree, and shall multiply like the cedar of Lebanon”* [Psalm 91:13]. Such a person is adorned with the fruits of the Holy Spirit: *“love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, self-control”* [Galatians 5:22-23].

If the root of a tree begins to rot, the tree itself will slowly begin to wither. So too: when faith in a person begins to fail, that person begins to fail in spiritual fruit. When the root of a tree rots away completely, the whole tree dries up; so too, when faith fails completely in a person, that person is utterly ruined. Such a one is alive and dead at once — the body lives, but the soul has died; he walks with one foot on the earth, while the other is already sinking into the gates of hell. His fruits are what he is within. His mind is crowded with thoughts unseemly, vain, and foul. From his heart proceed every lust and desire pleasing to a corrupted nature. His tongue is sharpened with much talk, slander, judging, calumny, and every kind of blasphemy. His eyes are full of fornication and unceasing sin. His ears are open only to foul, flesh-pleasing tales and songs. His hands are full of theft, bribery, murder. And so every part of him becomes an instrument of lawlessness. He turns wholly into sin: he thinks lawlessness, he speaks lawlessness, he does lawlessness. Of such people Wisdom says: *“They cannot sleep unless they have done evil”* [Proverbs 4:16]. Ah, what a fearful saying: *“They cannot sleep unless they have done evil.”*

So far can a wretched person grow accustomed to evil that he cannot even sleep unless he has done some wrong. The judge who takes bribes does not count as a day at all any day on which he failed to profit by unjust gain, and the night that follows is not without its own gnawing sorrow. The thief has no sleep — weariness and grief have seized his heart. Why? Because he failed to lay hold of another's goods. The adulterer laments that he did not manage to carry out his foul desire with this woman or that. Sleep departs from the head that nurses a grudge; within, his heart is torn, broken, tormented, wounded, because he did not yet take revenge on his rival. All these, and others like them, *“cannot sleep unless they have done evil.”*

sections.heading: Show me your faith by your works

pairs.en: To a person in such a state, exhortation and preaching do as much good as music does a deaf man, or speech a corpse. He listens to the holy Gospel, the word of God, as though it were a fable; he counts eternal torment and the kingdom of heaven as fiction. Someone will say: “How can it be that I do not believe the Gospel, when I hear it read in church almost every day?” Very well, brother — and I say to you, with the apostle James: *“Show me your faith by your works”* [James 2:18].

You believe the Gospel — why, then, do you not act, according to your faith, on what is written in the Gospel? You believe the Gospel — why, then, do you not obey the Gospel? You believe that God is everywhere, and therefore inseparably with you, wherever you may be and whatever you may be doing, knowing all things exactly — why, then, do you do what must on no account be done in the presence of God? When you stand before the Monarch, you stand with every reverence and fear, as is fitting, for his royal person itself demands it. God is a Great and Awesome King, who holds both your soul and your body in His hand; why, then, if you believe He is present with you, do you not render Him the same reverence and fear you show an earthly king when you stand before him? Is the reason perhaps that you see the earthly king, but do not see God? It is true you do not see God — nor can you. You do not see God with the eyes of the body, but you do see Him with the eyes of the soul, if you believe in Him. Such, then, is your faith!
You believe that God is a Righteous Judge — why, then, do you not tremble when you provoke Him with your sins? Such, then, is your faith!

You believe that God is the highest Good, and that He must be loved with the whole heart — why, then, do you not love Him as the greatest good? Why do you prefer some small pleasure to this highest good? Why do you do what is contrary to His holy will? One who loves another surely listens to him gladly in everything, and does his will in everything, so as not to grieve him. How can you love God and yet resist His will? Such, then, is your faith — and your love!

You believe that the Son of God came into the world for your sake, and endured fearful sufferings, and by them delivered you from eternal death — why, then, do you not please Him, according to your faith? If someone delivered you from bodily death by some means, you would surely do whatever he wished. Why, then, do you not do what Christ wishes, for His sake, if you believe He has delivered you from eternal death by so wondrous a means? Such, then, is your faith!

You believe that He will come in glory to judge the living and the dead — why, then, do you not appease Him beforehand with tears and repentance? Why do you not prepare for that Judgment? Those who must appear before a human court think well in advance how they might be acquitted at that trial. You believe you will stand before the judgment of God, where not only every evil deed but even every idle word will be examined, where you will be judged for deed, word, and thought — why, then, do you not only fail to appease beforehand that fearsome and incorruptible Judge, but do not even cease doing the very things for which you will be condemned at that trial before the whole world? Such, then, is your faith!

You believe the Gospel, which teaches that Christ counts as done to Himself whatever is given to the poor and needy for the sake of His holy name: *“Truly I say to you, inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these My brethren, you did it to Me”* [Matthew 25:40]. Why, then, will you not feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, take the stranger into your house, clothe the naked, visit the sick and those in prison? The buffoon and the jester who amuse you, the flatterer who shamelessly praises you, go away from you satisfied — but Christ, who promises you the kingdom of heaven, goes away with nothing?! You scatter your money with an open hand on banquets and music, yet you will not lower the rent, even a little, for peasants who sell their very last beast of burden just to pay it?! Your dogs — your beloved hunting hounds — grow fat from your table, while your poor servant is glad even of bread and water! You will lose a hundred roubles and more at cards in a single night and think nothing of it, yet you begrudge even a single rouble for ransoming captives or paying the debts of those sitting in prison. Is this your faith? Are these its fruits?!

You believe the Gospel, which promises eternal life and unending joy only to those who walk the narrow and sorrowful way — why, then, do you walk the broad way of pleasures and passions, which leads to destruction, according to the word of Christ [Matthew 7:13]? Such, then, is your faith!

A brave soldier who wishes to receive a high rank from his Monarch is not frightened by the crash and roar of death; he goes forward directly and exposes himself to every danger. A hard-working merchant who wants to gather temporal and perishable wealth is deterred neither by the danger of the sea, nor by robbers, nor by foreign peoples, nor by separation from wife and children, nor by wandering far from his sweet Fatherland. How much sweat the farmer pours out, scorched all summer long by the heat of the sun, for this one purpose only — to gather in the harvest he longs for! You see how much labour is undertaken for a merely perishable, almost illusory good? And you — if you believe in, and look for, an eternal good — why do you not undertake an equal labour for such a good? Such, then, is your faith!

No, my friend, such are not the fruits that Christian faith brings forth. As it is the nature of fire to warm, of water to water, of light to give light, so it is the nature of living faith to show forth good works. Do you wish to know what faith is, and what its fruits are? Look into the book of Genesis, chapters 15 and 22, and see how Abraham there, the father of all the faithful, in his advanced old age, at God's command, offers up Isaac his son as a sacrifice. Do you see how faith acted in that holy elder? His only son, his heir, given by the promise of God — the one of whom God had said, *“In Isaac shall your seed be called”* [Genesis 21:12] — he slaughters. *“For Abraham believed God, that He was able to raise him even from the dead”* [Hebrews 11:19]; and therefore, without wavering, he resolved to slay his own heir. And of him Scripture bears witness: *“Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness”* [Romans 4:3].

Read also the book of Exodus, and you will see how *“by faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season; esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompense of the reward”* [Hebrews 11:24-26]. It was faith that caused Moses to choose rather to suffer with God's people in the wilderness than to remain in Egyptian glory. He was firmly assured — strengthened by faith — that after undertaking such labours and sufferings there would follow a great and eternal reward from Christ.

And if you take the further trouble to read the book in which the lives of the saints, and the many and various sufferings of the martyrs, are recorded, you will learn still better how strong and effective faith is. There you will see that *“neither tribulation, nor distress, nor famine, nor nakedness, nor peril, nor sword, nor death”* could separate the soldiers of Christ *“from the love of God”* which is in Christ Jesus our Lord [Romans 8:35]. They were accounted *“as sheep for the slaughter”* [Psalm 43:23]. For Christ's sake they took bonds instead of ornaments, prisons instead of royal palaces, every reproach and slander instead of honour. They hastened to a shameful death, to be devoured by beasts, to be burned in fire, to be drowned in the sea, as if hurrying to a sweet wedding feast. Beatings, wounds, the tearing and breaking of their limbs, they bore as though it were happening to bodies not their own. And what compelled them to accept so many and such varied sufferings with joy, if not faith, and faith's own sister, love for Christ Jesus, and the reward, for that, of eternal and ineffable blessings in the heavenly palace?

You see, then, how they sealed their faith with their own blood and death. From these sufferers pass in your mind to those who suffered by their own free choice — the spiritual martyrs, the venerable fathers — and consider the struggle by which they contended against flesh and blood, against the world and the devil. What moved them to leave behind the beauty of this world and settle in the trackless wilderness, choosing to live with wild beasts rather than with men? What moved them to die daily to sin and the flesh, to subdue flesh to spirit by fasting, labour, hunger and thirst, to be washed with the hottest tears, to sigh from the depths of the heart, to groan without ceasing like a turtledove of the wilderness, to be scorched by the heat of the sun, to shiver from cold and frost, to wander naked over mountains, through caves, through the chasms of the earth? What, I ask, moved them to torment themselves by their own free choice, if not living and effective faith, and the love bound up with faith? All these martyrs I have named, receiving by faith the assurance that nothing worthy could ever be repaid for the love of God — by which He loved the world so much that He gave His only-begotten Son for it — and that *“the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us”* [Romans 8:18], gave themselves over to such varied and painful sufferings.

So you see, beloved, what the fruits of living faith are. You may also know this: that as a tree is known by its fruit, so faith is known by its works. Faith lives, and intercedes for eternal life, in the one in whom its fruits appear. There is no living faith in the one in whom no works proceeding from faith can be seen — as the apostle James wrote: *“As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also”* [James 2:26].

And if faith without works is dead, then in truth it is no faith at all. For what the soul is to the body, faith is to the soul. The body lives while the soul is in it; but once the soul departs, the body is already dead — unfeeling, unhearing, unseeing, without scent, without motion. The soul lives while faith lives in it. When faith ceases to be, the soul, too, has already died, for it too has no spiritual movement left in it. And a person who has such a soul is like an idol: *“they have eyes and see not; they have ears and hear not; they have nostrils and smell not”* [Psalm 113:13-14] — that is, he has no wish to see or hear anything spiritual or saving. For he is wholly carnal and unspiritual: *“the natural man,”* says the apostle, *“receives not the things of the Spirit of God”* [1 Corinthians 2:14]. And this is what the same apostle means when he says: *“But without faith it is impossible to please God”* [Hebrews 11:6].

sections.heading: Not every good deed is from faith

pairs.en: For many people do good, but not from faith, and therefore cannot please God. Many abstain from murder, from theft, from robbery, from usury, from slander, but do so out of fear of man, afraid of civil punishment, and not out of fear of God — and this is not from faith. Many keep themselves from impurity, but for human shame and not for fear of God — that is, not from faith — for such people secretly dare to do in private what it is *“a shame even to speak of”* [Ephesians 5:12]. Some appear meek and gentle, but only for the sake of a peaceful and easy life among people. This is human wisdom, and therefore not from faith. Some do every kind of good to their neighbours, but only so as to be loved by them, and this is not from faith. Others give much in alms, build churches and almshouses, but only in order to be seen by people, and this is not from faith. Some multiply and lengthen their prayers *“that they may be seen of men”* [Matthew 23:5], and this is not from faith. Many fast a great deal, but only *“to appear unto men to fast”* [Matthew 6:16], and this is not from faith.

All these, and others like them, since they do good not for God's sake, do it not from faith, and therefore cannot please God by it. They act either for the sake of vain glory, or for some other reason, but not for the glory of God. For how can what is not done for His sake be pleasing to God?
So far I have told you what living faith is, and what dead faith is. Now I will set before you the source of living faith, and by what means it is increased.

Living faith is a gift of God, a kind of divine seed which is sown into every person at Baptism. It is this seed from which a person is said to be born of God. Of this the holy apostle John the Theologian speaks: *“Whosoever is born of God does not commit sin, for His seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he is born of God”* [1 John 3:9].

sections.heading: The word of God waters the seed

pairs.en: As seed sown in the ground grows and is nourished by moisture, so the seed of divine faith, sown in the soil of the human heart, grows and is nourished by the moisture of the word of God, as the apostle Paul says: *“Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God”* [Romans 10:17]. *“The word of God is living,”* says the same God-inspired teacher, *“and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart”* [Hebrews 4:12]. And again the same apostle: *“All Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works”* [2 Timothy 3:16-17].

sections.heading: What the word of God shows us of God

pairs.en: The word of God shows us God as One in Essence yet Three in Persons, and therefore incomprehensible — and therefore He is not to be probed and questioned. The word of God shows Him to us as Almighty, and therefore His help alone is to be sought. The word of God shows Him as caring for all, and therefore hope is to be placed in Him. The word of God shows Him as one who cannot lie, and therefore He is to be believed without doubt. The word of God shows Him as Righteous, rendering to each according to his deeds, and therefore He is to be feared. The word of God shows Him as Great, and therefore we must humble ourselves before Him. The word of God shows Him as Everywhere Present, seeing all our deeds, words and thoughts, and therefore we must walk before Him, as before a fearsome King, with all fear and caution, doing, saying and thinking only what is pleasing to His will. The word of God shows Him as All-Good, and therefore He is to be loved. The word of God shows Him as Merciful to repentant sinners, and therefore sinners must flee to Him with repentance and sorrow. The word of God shows Him as coming to judge the living and the dead, and therefore we must prepare for His Judgment.

So, too, in everything else that concerns faith and its fruits, the word of God shows, teaches, demonstrates, and assures us. In this way the word of God causes faith to grow and increase in the human heart.

The word of God must be heard or read not carelessly, but with all diligence, attention, and reflection. It is not enough merely to open the ears to hear it; the heart, too, must be opened to receive the word of God. We must hear the word of God with those ears which Christ requires in many places in the Gospel, saying: *“He who has ears to hear, let him hear”* [Matthew 13:43]! From this it follows that whoever does not read, or does not listen attentively to, the word of God, cannot keep the faith or show forth its fruits. Such people fall into every kind of error and confusion; they can do nothing good or salutary for their souls, however good they may appear. And in order that the word of God may work its power and effect in the heart, we must earnestly pray to its Author, with David: *“Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of Your law”* [Psalm 118:18].

sections.heading: Read the lives of the saints

pairs.en: Besides this, it is needful often to read and to ponder the lives of God's saints, who excelled in faith and in its fruits, so that we may the more readily imitate their faith. For truly it is written of this: *“Whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning,”* says the holy apostle Paul [Romans 15:4]. Thus, if we meditate on the law of the Lord and pray earnestly to the Author of that law, we shall surely all *“come to the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ”* [Ephesians 4:13]. Amen.
